why.correct: Arginine (positive) kept 44.5 of 48.0, about 93%. Glutamate (negative) gave 0.6 and alanine (no charge) gave 3.9, both below 10% of the original. The charge at 102, not just its presence, matters.
options: This matches the table: the positive-for-positive swap kept most of the output, while losing (alanine) or reversing (glutamate) the charge dropped it below a tenth.
Variant 1 kept about 93% of the original output, so a change at 102 did not always cut it sharply; it depended on the new side chain's charge.
With T the three variants stayed near the original (1.8-2.4 against 2.1), while with S two of them collapsed, so the effects were not proportional.
Alanine is smaller than lysine and arginine is larger, yet alanine cut output far more; size of the side chain does not explain the pattern.

why.correct: Percentage of original = (variant ÷ original) × 100 = (3.9 ÷ 48.0) × 100 = 8.125, which rounds to 8.1%.

Like charges repel. Lysine's positive side chain attracts S's negative end; glutamate's negative side chain pushes it away. T has no charge at that end, so it neither gained from lysine nor suffers from glutamate.
options: Charge explains both results: reversing the charge turns attraction into repulsion for S, while uncharged T is unaffected either way.
The stem says S and T have the same shape and size, so a size-based block would affect both equally.
An unfolded enzyme would lose its active site for both substrates; T's near-normal output shows the enzyme is still folded.
The original enzyme forms 48.0 units from S and only 2.1 from T, so S, not T, is the substrate the active site matches best.

why.correct: Variant 5 cut output with both S (to 1.1) and T (to 0.4). A charge effect would spare uncharged T, as variant 2 showed; a change that hurts both points to shape: a bulky side chain filling the pocket.
options: Both substrates are affected, which fits a shape change in the pocket rather than a charge change, which spared T in variant 2.
The table lists tryptophan's side chain as nonpolar, not charged, and a charge effect would not have hurt uncharged T.
The stem says position 100 lines the active site, and every trial used the same amount of enzyme.
The data show product formation only; nothing measures binding strength, and a pocket filled by a large side chain is the simpler explanation.

why.correct: Variant 4 changed a surface amino acid and kept 47.2 of 48.0. That shows the swapping process itself does not wreck the enzyme, which strengthens the case that the active-site swaps cause the drops.
options: A swap far from the active site barely changed output, which helps tie the big effects of the other swaps to the active site.
Output fell from 48.0 to 47.2, under 2%, so removing serine 245 had almost no effect.
Variant 4 is an enzyme with one changed amino acid; a no-enzyme tube would be the negative control, and none is shown.
The S-versus-T difference is the same in the original enzyme, so variant 4 adds nothing new about substrate charge.

why.correct: The gap shrinks from 2.6 nm to 0.9 nm only when G binds. The enzyme itself changes shape as the substrate binds: induced fit.
options: The lobes move closer by 1.7 nm when G binds, the enzyme shape change that defines induced fit.
A rigid lock would keep the gap the same with or without G; the gap clearly changes.
The measurement is between two points on the enzyme, so a change in that distance shows the enzyme moving.
Water is in every sample and is small enough to enter, yet the gap stays at 2.6 nm; molecule L also leaves it mostly open.

why.correct: An –OH group is polar and can hydrogen bond with a polar side chain. Replacing it with –H removes that contact. With less of the right attraction, the lobes do not close and the substrate's bonds are not held in place to react.
options: Losing one polar contact is enough to stop the shape change, showing that both shape and chemical matching matter.
The table says L is the same size as G, so it can enter the cleft as G does.
Nothing in the data shows tighter binding; an open gap fits weak, partial binding better.
Swapping –OH for –H adds no charge, and the gap (2.3 nm) is smaller than with water alone, not larger.

why.correct: Closing happens around the substrate. If the cleft is already closed, G cannot enter, so the enzyme-substrate complex cannot form and little product is made.
options: The substrate must get in before the lobes close; a cleft that is already shut keeps it out.
Being in the bound shape is useless without the substrate inside; the closed lobes block entry.
In the data the gap changes when G binds, before product forms, so it matters for binding.
Water entering the open cleft did not stop the original enzyme from working, so keeping it out offers no gain.

why.correct: A rigid mold would not move. The 1.7 nm change shows the enzyme's shape changes when G binds.
options: This is direct evidence that the enzyme's shape changes on binding, which a rigid mold could not do.
A molecule too big to fit makes no product under either model, so this cannot tell them apart.
Water gives no product under either model; it says nothing about whether the enzyme moves.
Averaging repeated measurements makes the data more reliable but says nothing about rigidity.

why.correct: Tube 1 reached 11.6 mM glucose. Tubes 2 and 3 stayed at 0.2 and 0.1 mM, the same as the no-enzyme tube (0.1), so maltose and sucrose were not broken.
options: The maltose and sucrose tubes match the no-enzyme background, so only lactose was broken.
Maltose and sucrose both contain glucose, but their tubes show no more glucose than the background.
Maltose and sucrose show essentially nothing, while lactose released over 11 mM; the difference is not slight.
The boiled-enzyme tube (0.1 mM) matches the tube with no enzyme, so boiling stopped the breakdown.

why.correct: Glucose made by the enzyme = 11.6 − 0.1 = 11.5 mM. Each lactose broken releases one glucose, so 11.5 mM of lactose was broken down.
Boiling denatures the enzyme and destroys the active site's shape. If something else in the sample, unharmed by heat, were breaking lactose, tube 4 would still show glucose. It does not.
options: Boiling unfolds the protein; the loss of glucose production ties the effect to the intact enzyme.
Only the enzyme was boiled, before it was added; the lactose was not heated, and tube 5 shows lactose alone makes no glucose.
Tube 4 contains lactose, so any glucose there could come from breakdown; it is not a measure of glucose in the enzyme sample alone.
The enzyme was boiled before the test, which denatures it; tube 4's result shows it stopped working.

why.correct: Galactose and glucose have the same atoms but one –OH points a different way. The active site's polar side chains form hydrogen bonds with the –OH groups in the positions lactose has, so only lactose binds and is held in the right position to react.
options: Specificity depends on fine details of shape and polar contacts, such as which way each –OH group points.
The stem says the two are almost the same size; glucose and galactose have the same number of atoms.
These sugars are uncharged; the matching here is about –OH positions and hydrogen bonding, not ionic charge.
Each tube held only one disaccharide, and enzymes come out of a reaction unchanged and act again.

why.correct: A catalyst speeds a reaction and is unchanged at the end, so one enzyme molecule can act on many substrate molecules.
options: This is the definition of a catalyst: faster reaction, catalyst unchanged.
The products' atoms come from the substrate; the enzyme's atoms stay in the enzyme.
An enzyme that broke down as it worked could act only once; enzymes act again and again.
An enzyme speeds up a reaction that could happen anyway; the products are the same with or without it.

why.correct: A negative group is attracted to the positive side chain, and a nonpolar ring clusters with the nonpolar wall. Both parts of the substrate match the active site.
options: Both regions match: opposite charges attract and nonpolar groups cluster together.
A positive group would be repelled by the positive side chain at the base.
The charge matches, but polar –OH groups would sit against a nonpolar wall instead of a matching surface.
With no charged group, nothing in this molecule is attracted to the positive side chain, and its polar groups do not match the nonpolar wall.

why.correct: The active site's shape comes from the folding of the whole protein. Losing an attraction that holds two parts together can loosen the fold and distort the active site.
options: Distant amino acids hold the overall shape, and the active site's shape depends on that overall shape.
The active site is formed by the whole folded chain; distant contacts that hold the fold can change it.
A distorted active site matches the substrate worse; it does not become a better match for other molecules.
Position 310 is far from the active site and not shaped to hold the substrate, so the substrate has no reason to bind there.

why.correct: High heat denatures the protein: it breaks hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions that hold the fold. Here the shape did not come back on cooling, so the active site no longer fits the substrate.
options: Denaturation unfolds the protein and wrecks the active site's shape; this enzyme did not refold.
Heating to 70 °C unfolds proteins but does not hydrolyze peptide bonds; the chain stays intact.
37 °C is the normal temperature for a human enzyme, so slow movement cannot be the reason.
Enzymes do not store energy that runs out; they work by holding the substrate in the active site.

why.correct: Specificity covers more than which molecule binds: it also covers how it is held. Different active sites position different parts of glucose next to their reactive side chains, so different bonds change.
options: Different active sites grip the same substrate differently, so different bonds break or form.
Glucose has the same structure in solution near both enzymes; the difference lies in the enzymes.
Both make products from glucose, so both act as catalysts.
Identical active sites would hold glucose the same way and make the same product, wherever they were.

why.correct: Weak, reversible attractions hold the substrate (so it can leave as product), and induced fit tightens the grip.
options: Weak attractions hold the substrate firmly enough to react, yet let the products go.
This is induced fit: binding shifts the active site's shape.
Products are released and the enzyme is unchanged, so the enzyme's atoms are not built into the product.
The complex is short-lived; after the products leave, the enzyme binds another substrate.
Size is not enough: the substrate must match the active site's shape and chemical character.

why.correct: What makes an enzyme work is a folded shape that forms a specific binding site. RNA can fold into such shapes using base pairing and other weak attractions.
options: Specific 3-D shape and a matching binding site are what any biological catalyst needs.
RNA is made of nucleotides, not amino acids, so it has no amino acid side chains.
Neither kind of enzyme is bonded permanently to its substrate; the products are released.
Attracting any negative molecule would mean no specificity; real active sites match particular substrates.

why.correct: The same reaction implies the same substrate and a similar active site. Changes elsewhere can affect how firmly the protein holds its fold, for example in cold, high-pressure water, without changing what it binds.
options: Conserved active sites explain the shared reaction; other changes can tune stability of the fold.
The stem says both catalyze the same reaction, and many different sequences can fold into similar active sites.
None of the 40 changes is in the active site, and the stem says both catalyze the same reaction.
Amino acids away from the active site help hold the fold, so they can affect stability even if they never touch the substrate.

why.correct: A look-alike molecule takes up active sites without reacting, so fewer sites are free for the real substrate and product forms more slowly. The enzymes themselves are still there.

variables.name: Number of active sites holding the substrate at any moment
variables.why: Some active sites are occupied by the drug, so fewer are free to hold the substrate at a given moment.

variables.name: Product formed per minute
variables.why: Product forms only from substrate in an active site; with fewer sites holding substrate, less product forms each minute.

variables.name: Total number of enzyme molecules in the tube
variables.why: The drug binds the enzymes but does not destroy them or add new ones, so the count is unchanged.

why.correct: Rate = change in amount ÷ change in time = (9.0 mL − 0.0 mL) ÷ (30 s − 0 s) = 0.30 mL/s.
26.0 mL of a possible 27 mL has been collected, so the reactant is almost gone. With little hydrogen peroxide left, fewer molecules reach an active site each second.
options: The total collected nearly equals the maximum, which shows the reactant, not the enzyme, has run out.
Enzymes are not used up; each catalase molecule breaks down huge numbers of hydrogen peroxide molecules.
Nothing in the data tests oxygen's effect on the enzyme; the slowdown is explained by the reactant running out.
Enzymes do not supply energy to reactants; they lower the activation energy.

why.correct: With no catalyst, hydrogen peroxide still breaks down very slowly (0.9 mL in 180 s). That baseline shows how much each catalyst adds.
options: This flask gives the uncatalyzed rate, the reference point for every comparison.
Only 0.9 mL formed in 3 minutes, so breakdown on its own is very slow.
The boiled extract tests something different: whether the extract's effect needs a folded enzyme.
The water flask measures oxygen produced from hydrogen peroxide, not oxygen dissolving.

why.correct: Manganese dioxide made 16.0 mL in 180 s, against 0.9 mL with water, so it catalyzes the reaction. Its first-30-s rate (0.10 mL/s) is a third of fresh extract's (0.30 mL/s) with the amounts used.
options: Both catalysts beat the water flask; fresh extract was faster at first with these amounts.
A catalyst is anything that speeds a reaction and is unchanged; non-living catalysts exist, and this one clearly sped the reaction.
Boiled extract (0.8 mL) did no better than water (0.9 mL), so it did not speed the reaction at all.
A catalyst does not change the energy a reaction releases; it changes only how fast the reaction goes.

why.correct: Catalase comes out of each reaction unchanged, so it can break down the new hydrogen peroxide and oxygen production jumps from almost nothing. It will not quite match the first 30 seconds, because the new peroxide is mixed into liquid already in the flask, so its concentration is lower than at the start.
options: The enzyme is reused; fresh reactant makes the rate jump from almost zero, though not quite back to the starting rate.
Enzymes are not consumed, so the catalase still works after the first batch is gone.
Each catalase molecule can act millions of times; there is no small limit on uses.
The volume roughly doubles, which dilutes both catalase and peroxide somewhat, but the flask goes from almost no reactant to plenty, so the rate rises rather than falls.

why.correct: Activation energy = peak energy − energy of the reactants = 115 − 40 = 75 kJ/mol.
Without the enzyme: 115 − 40 = 75 kJ/mol. With it: 70 − 40 = 30 kJ/mol. Percent decrease = (75 − 30) ÷ 75 × 100 = 60%.
Both curves start at 40 and end at 15 kJ/mol; only the peak differs (115 against 70). The energy released, 40 − 15 = 25 kJ/mol, is the same.
options: Same start, same end, lower peak: that is what an enzyme does.
Both curves end at 15 kJ/mol, so the products have the same energy with or without the enzyme.
Both curves start at 40 kJ/mol; the enzyme does not change the reactants' energy.
The product level is 15 kJ/mol on both curves; only the peak moves.

why.correct: Going backward, the molecules start at the product level (15) and climb to the same peak: 115 − 15 = 100 kJ/mol without the enzyme, 70 − 15 = 55 with it. The enzyme lowers both barriers by 45 kJ/mol, so it speeds both directions.
options: The peak is shared by both directions, so lowering it lowers both barriers by the same 45 kJ/mol.
The backward reaction passes through the same transition state, which the enzyme stabilizes; the graph shows the lower peak serves both directions.
Those values are measured from the reactant level (40); the backward reaction starts at the product level (15).
The peak is lower with the enzyme, so the climb from the products is smaller, not larger.

why.correct: The peak is the transition state: bonds partly broken and partly formed, the highest-energy, least stable point on the path.
options: The top of the hill is the transition state, between reactants and products.
Products appear on the right side of the graph, after the peak, at 15 kJ/mol.
The enzyme adds no energy; the curve with the enzyme is lower, not higher.
The products' energy is the flat level on the right (15 kJ/mol), not the peak.

why.correct: All six batches gave 4.6-4.8 mmol, and the values move up and down rather than falling steadily.
options: The range is narrow (4.6-4.8 mmol) with no downward trend.
Batch 6 (4.7 mmol) is almost the same as batch 1 (4.8 mmol), not half.
Output did not rise, and enzymes do not learn; each binding is a separate event.
Batch 1 (4.8) was among the highest and batch 6 (4.7) was not the highest.

why.correct: Output stayed steady over six batches, and the beads still held 2.0 mg of enzyme at the end. The enzyme was reused, not consumed.
options: Steady output and unchanged enzyme mass both show the enzyme was reused.
The 4.8 values are amounts of glucose in mmol, not energies; the setup measures no energy.
The beads held 2.0 mg before and after, so no enzyme was lost into the product.
Only sucrose was tested, so the data say nothing about other sugars.

why.correct: Glucose per enzyme = moles of glucose ÷ moles of enzyme = (2.84 × 10⁻² mol) ÷ (7.4 × 10⁻⁹ mol) ≈ 3.8 × 10⁶, about 4 million.
options: 2.84 × 10⁻² ÷ 7.4 × 10⁻⁹ ≈ 3.8 × 10⁶: millions of reactions per enzyme molecule.
This uses millimoles of glucose (28.4) against micromoles of enzyme; convert both to moles first.
One product per enzyme would mean the enzyme is used up; the steady output shows it is not.
This is a thousand times too high; check the powers of ten when dividing.

why.correct: Activation energy is the climb from the reactants up to the transition state, the energy barrier every reaction must clear.
options: This is the definition: the barrier between reactants and the transition state.
That is the difference between reactants and products, which an enzyme does not change.
Enzymes add no energy; they lower the barrier.
The products' energy is the end level of the diagram, not the barrier.

why.correct: Whether a reaction releases energy and how fast it runs are different questions. A high activation energy keeps this reaction extremely slow, even though it releases energy, without a catalyst.
options: A high barrier makes the reaction slow even though it releases energy overall.
The stem says the reaction releases energy; what stops it is the barrier, not the overall energy change.
Sucrose is the reactant here; it is broken into glucose and fructose.
No glucose or fructose is forming in the bowl in measurable amounts, so there is nothing to re-form sucrose.

why.correct: Higher temperature means faster molecules, so a bigger share has enough energy to reach the transition state. An enzyme changes the path so less energy is needed.
options: Heat changes the molecules' energy; the enzyme changes the height of the hill.
This reverses the two: heating supplies energy; enzymes lower the barrier and supply none.
Neither heating nor an enzyme changes which products a given reaction makes.
Both can speed either kind of reaction; neither choice depends on whether energy is released.

why.correct: Product added per minute: 12, 10, 7, 4, 2 µmol. The rate, the slope, is steepest at the start and falls as the remaining substrate drops.
options: The per-minute gains fall from 12 to 2 µmol, so the rate is highest at first.
35 ÷ 5 = 7 is the average rate; the actual rate changes from 12 down to 2 µmol/min.
The amount of product rises, but the amount added each minute (the rate) falls.
The last minute added only 2 µmol, the smallest gain; rate is the change per minute, not the total.

why.correct: Active sites bring reactants together in the right orientation, strain the substrate toward the transition state, and provide side chains whose charges or polar groups help bonds break and form.
options: Correct orientation means fewer chance meetings are wasted.
Strain pushes the substrate partway toward the transition state.
Charged and polar side chains can give or take hydrogen ions or stabilize charges as bonds change.
Enzymes do not heat their substrates; they change the path, not the temperature.
The products' energy is the same with or without the enzyme.
The enzyme comes out unchanged, so it cannot be spending its own bonds.

why.correct: An enzyme lowers the activation energy and so raises the rate. It changes neither the energy released nor its own amount.

variables.name: Activation energy of the reaction
variables.why: The enzyme's active site makes the transition state easier to reach, lowering the barrier.

variables.name: Energy released per mole of reactant that reacts
variables.why: The reactants and products have the same energy with or without the enzyme, so the energy released is unchanged.

variables.name: Time needed to make 1 mmol of product
variables.why: A lower barrier means more molecules react per second, so the same amount of product forms sooner.

variables.name: Amount of enzyme in the tube after 1 hour
variables.why: Enzymes are not used up; after releasing the products each enzyme molecule has its original structure.

why.correct: Enzymes change the path, not the start and end points. A reaction that does not happen on its own because it would need an energy input still needs that input with an enzyme; one that can happen just happens faster.
options: Enzymes change speed only; the reactants, products and overall energy change are fixed.
Uncatalyzed reactions have a finite barrier; the water flask in a catalase experiment still makes a little oxygen.
Enzymes supply no energy; reactions that need energy get it by being linked to other reactions, a topic for 3.4.
The products of a reaction are the same with or without the enzyme.

why.correct: At 32 mM: no inhibitor 47.1, X 42.1 (about 89%), Y 23.5 (about 50%).
options: X nearly catches up (42.1 against 47.1) while Y stays near half (23.5).
At 32 mM, X is at about 89% of the uninhibited rate, not half.
This reverses the two inhibitors: Y is the one stuck near half.
Y still halves the rate at 32 mM, so the inhibitors do change it there.

why.correct: Extra substrate outcompetes a competitive inhibitor, so X's curve keeps climbing toward the uninhibited maximum. Y levels off near half: extra substrate cannot undo a shape change at an allosteric site.
options: The pattern at high substrate tells them apart: X catches up, Y's plateau stays low.
Lowering the rate most at low substrate is what a competitive inhibitor does, because there the inhibitor wins most of the competition.
Every curve levels off eventually; what matters is the height of the plateau, and Y's is about half.
Equal rates at one concentration do not identify the type; the curves separate sharply at high substrate.

why.correct: Rate with Y ÷ rate with no inhibitor × 100 = 20.0 ÷ 40.0 × 100 = 50%.
X's curve is still climbing toward the uninhibited maximum of about 50 µmol/min; Y's has nearly leveled off near 25 µmol/min, half the maximum.
options: Following each curve's trend: X keeps closing the gap, Y stays at its lower plateau.
Substrate can outcompete only an inhibitor that competes for the active site; Y's plateau has already flattened.
An inhibitor lowers the rate; nothing in the data suggests Y could make the enzyme faster than no inhibitor.
Substrate does not denature enzymes; the uninhibited curve keeps rising toward its maximum.

why.correct: An inhibitor at an allosteric site changes the active site's shape. Substrate cannot compete with something that is not in the active site, so the maximum rate stays lower.
options: A noncompetitive inhibitor removes working enzyme without competing, so the plateau drops.
An inhibitor that substrate eventually pushes out is competitive; that describes X, whose curve catches up.
Nothing in the setup suggests Y reacts with the substrate; the pattern matches binding to the enzyme.
An inhibited enzyme still lowers the barrier for the substrate it does handle; Y reduces how many enzymes work well.

why.correct: Read the middle column: 55 µmol/min at 45 °C is the highest rate measured at a holding temperature.
options: At 25 °C the rate was 18, the lowest of the first four.
37 °C gave 40, lower than the 55 at 45 °C.
45 °C gave the highest rate, 55 µmol/min.
By 50 °C the rate had already fallen to 34.

why.correct: Returned to 37 °C, the sample matched the undamaged control. The enzyme was intact; at 25 °C there were simply fewer collisions with enough energy.
options: Full recovery at 37 °C shows the enzyme's shape was intact; the slowdown came from slower molecules.
Being faster than damaged samples does not show this sample was undamaged.
This states a general idea but cites no data from this enzyme; the third column is the direct test.
A low rate at 25 °C could come from damage or from slow molecules; this comparison cannot tell which.

why.correct: Recovery from 6 to 14 shows that some denaturation reversed (renaturation). Recovering to 14, not 40, shows most of the enzyme stayed denatured.
options: Partial recovery fits partial renaturation with lasting damage to the rest.
Full recovery would bring the rate back to about 40; it reached only 14.
A tube of purified enzyme has no cells to make new protein.
If the enzyme were unchanged it would recover to about 40 at 37 °C, like the 25 °C sample; it did not.

why.correct: Measuring all samples under the same conditions shows what each sample can still do. A sample that recovers was only slowed; one that does not was damaged.
options: The second measurement isolates lasting damage, because conditions are now identical for all samples.
The holding temperature is the independent variable; time was held constant, not varied.
The optimum comes from the rate measured at each temperature, the middle column.
Substrates are usually small molecules, not folded proteins; the enzyme is what may have changed.

why.correct: Recovered rate ÷ control rate × 100 = 14 ÷ 40 × 100 = 35%.
At pH 5, pepsin is at 12% and trypsin at 22%: both above 10%. At pH 4 trypsin is at 8%; at pH 6 pepsin is at 2%.
options: At pH 3 trypsin is at 2%.
At pH 4 trypsin is at 8%, below 10%.
Pepsin 12% and trypsin 22%: both above 10%.
At pH 6 pepsin has fallen to 2%.

why.correct: The graph shows pepsin at 0% at pH 8. With far fewer hydrogen ions, side chains lose hydrogen ions and change charge, altering the active site and the fold.
options: Pepsin's rate is 0% at pH 8 in the data; changed side-chain charges explain why.
pH 8 has a million times fewer hydrogen ions than pH 2, not more.
Enzymes bind and release substrate continuously; a change in pH affects every new binding.
Each enzyme has its own optimal pH; pepsin's is 2, and it does not work at trypsin's optimum.

why.correct: Side chains such as –COO⁻ and –NH₃⁺ gain or lose hydrogen ions as pH changes. Active-site charges that bind the substrate, and ionic attractions that hold the fold, work best at pH 8.
options: Gaining or losing hydrogen ions changes charges on either side of the optimum.
A rate cannot be pushed above its maximum by pH; the curve falls on both sides because conditions are worse.
The data measure the enzyme's rate; nothing suggests the substrate stops dissolving.
The graph shows trypsin above zero from pH 3 to 10, for example 55% at pH 6.

why.correct: Pepsin's optimum is pH 2 and trypsin's pH 8. Each pH unit is a tenfold change, so 6 units is 10⁶ = 1,000,000 times.
A cofactor is a non-protein helper the enzyme needs; metal ions such as zinc are common cofactors.
options: The zinc is a helper the enzyme needs, which is the definition of a cofactor.
A substrate is changed by the enzyme; the zinc stays and helps with each reaction.
An inhibitor lowers the rate; the enzyme needs this zinc in order to work.
A product is made by the reaction and released; the zinc stays bound.

why.correct: EDTA lowered the rate by taking away the cofactor. Once there is more Mg²⁺ than EDTA can bind, free Mg²⁺ returns to the enzyme and it works again.
options: Replacing the missing cofactor restores the enzyme's function.
EDTA binds metal ions; it does not unfold proteins, and the rate loss is explained by the missing cofactor.
A cofactor helps the enzyme and is not used up; it is not the substrate.
Once every enzyme has its cofactor, extra Mg²⁺ adds nothing; the rate returns to about its starting value.

why.correct: On the plateau, nearly every active site is busy, so the amount of enzyme is the limiting factor. More enzyme means more active sites and a higher rate.
options: Enzyme is the limiting factor on the plateau; adding it adds active sites.
The active sites are already saturated, so extra substrate has little effect.
An inhibitor lowers the rate.
Cooling slows collisions and lowers the rate.

why.correct: A reversible inhibitor lets go and diffuses away, so the enzyme recovers. An irreversible inhibitor is bound for good, usually by a covalent bond, so the enzyme stays inhibited.
options: Activity that does not return after the free inhibitor is removed points to permanent binding.
Recovery shows the inhibitor let go: that is reversible inhibition.
Being overcome by substrate is the sign of a competitive, reversible inhibitor.
How fast small molecules cross the bag says nothing about how the inhibitor binds the enzyme.

why.correct: pH is the independent variable and the rate is the dependent variable. Everything else that affects rate, such as temperature and the amounts of enzyme and substrate, must stay the same.
options: These all affect rate, so they are controlled variables.
pH is the variable being tested; it cannot be held constant.
pH is tested and rate is measured; neither is held constant.
Rate is the dependent variable, the thing being measured.

why.correct: At saturation the enzyme amount limits the rate: more enzyme raises it, extra substrate does not, and inhibitors or cooling lower it.

variables.name: Doubling the substrate concentration
variables.why: The active sites are already saturated, so extra substrate has nowhere to bind and the rate stays at the maximum.

variables.name: Doubling the enzyme concentration
variables.why: Enzyme is the limiting factor on the plateau; twice the active sites gives about twice the rate.

variables.name: Adding a noncompetitive inhibitor
variables.why: It binds an allosteric site and changes the enzyme's shape, removing working enzyme; substrate cannot reverse it.

variables.name: Cooling the reaction to 27 °C
variables.why: Molecules move more slowly, so fewer collisions have enough energy to react.

why.correct: Binding at an allosteric site changes the enzyme's shape. A molecule that speeds the enzyme up holds the active site in its working shape; an allosteric inhibitor does the reverse.
options: Allosteric regulation can work in either direction; this molecule favors the active shape.
It binds away from the active site and is not changed into product.
A molecule that binds away from the active site does not compete for it.
Enzymes and their regulators do not add energy; they change shape and lower the barrier.

why.correct: The maximum rate depends on how many working active sites there are. A noncompetitive inhibitor and permanent denaturation both reduce working enzyme, and substrate cannot fix either.
options: It takes enzyme out of action in a way extra substrate cannot undo.
Permanently denatured enzymes have no working active site, so fewer remain.
Enough substrate outcompetes it, so the same maximum is still reached.
The maximum is defined with unlimited substrate, so the substrate level does not change it.
More enzyme raises the maximum rate.

why.correct: Both molecules use the same active site. With plenty of fomepizole, most active sites hold it at any moment, so methanol is converted slowly and leaves the body before much toxic product forms.
options: A molecule that competes with the substrate for the active site is a competitive inhibitor; giving enough of it protects the patient.
The stem says fomepizole binds the active site, not an allosteric site.
A permanently denatured enzyme would not depend on the drug staying present; nothing suggests the drug unfolds the enzyme.
The treatment acts on the enzyme, stopping the toxic product from forming, not on the product afterward.

why.correct: In the first minute 55 °C wins (18 against 10 µmol), but by 5-10 minutes it adds almost nothing (40 to 41) while 37 °C keeps going. The hot enzyme is losing its shape over time.
options: A fast start then a stall at a lower total points to the enzyme failing, not the substrate.
Both tubes started with the same substrate, and the 37 °C tube made 90 µmol, so substrate was still available when the 55 °C tube stalled near 41.
Steady production at 37 °C shows a working enzyme; denaturing would slow it down.
Nothing in the data shows product breaking down; an enzyme losing its shape explains the stall more simply.

why.correct: Exergonic reactions release energy and have a negative ΔG: reactions 1 (−30.5), 4 (−43.0) and 5 (−13.8).
options: All three have a negative ΔG, so they release energy.
Reactions 2 and 3 have a positive ΔG: they are endergonic.
Reaction 5 also has a negative ΔG (−13.8), so it is exergonic too.
Reactions 2 and 3 are endergonic; only reaction 5 of these three releases energy.

why.correct: Coupled ΔG = ΔG of reaction 1 + ΔG of reaction 2 = −30.5 + 14.2 = −16.3 kJ/mol. The negative total means the coupled process releases energy and can go.
Coupled with creatine phosphate: −43.0 + 30.5 = −12.5 kJ/mol, negative, so it goes. With glucose 6-phosphate: −13.8 + 30.5 = +16.7 kJ/mol, positive, so it does not.
options: Creatine phosphate releases more than 30.5 kJ/mol; glucose 6-phosphate releases less. Muscles use creatine phosphate to remake ATP quickly.
A negative ΔG is not enough: it must outweigh the +30.5 needed. −13.8 + 30.5 is still positive.
Endergonic reactions go when coupled to a larger exergonic one; creatine phosphate is large enough.
The total must be negative; coupling glucose 6-phosphate breakdown with ATP synthesis gives +16.7 kJ/mol.

why.correct: Coupling works through a shared intermediate. Phosphorylating glutamate makes a high-energy, unstable molecule; its reaction with NH₃ releases the phosphate and is exergonic.
options: Phosphate transfer to a reactant (phosphorylation) is the usual way ATP drives a reaction.
Heat spreads out and cannot drive a specific reaction; the energy is passed on through the phosphate.
An allosteric effect changes the enzyme's rate, not the ΔG of the reaction it catalyzes.
Enzymes come out of reactions unchanged and do not store energy.

why.correct: −30.5 + 45.0 = +14.5 kJ/mol, still positive. Coupling to two ATP (−61.0 + 45.0 = −16.0) or to creatine phosphate plus ATP would make the total negative.
options: The coupled total must be negative; one ATP leaves it positive.
ATP hydrolysis supplies about 30.5 kJ/mol, which is not enough for a +45.0 reaction.
Enzymes change the rate, not the ΔG; a positive total stays positive.
Endergonic reactions go all the time in cells when coupled to enough energy release.

why.correct: Isoleucine lowers the rate from 100% to 4% across the range; valine leaves it at 97-100%.
options: Steep fall with isoleucine, almost none with valine.
Valine leaves the rate at 97-100%, while isoleucine cuts it to 4%.
Isoleucine lowers the rate; it does not raise it.
The rate already falls to 82% at 0.1 mM and 45% at 0.5 mM.

why.correct: Changing one amino acid at the allosteric site makes enzyme 1 ignore isoleucine (93-99%), so isoleucine must act at that site. Valine, though similar, does not fit it.
options: The changed-enzyme column ties isoleucine's effect to the allosteric site.
The changed enzyme differs only at the allosteric site, yet isoleucine stops working on it, so the active site is not where isoleucine acts.
Denaturation would not be undone by a change at the allosteric site, and a substance that denatures proteins would affect the changed enzyme too.
The experiments had plenty of threonine, and the allosteric-site result points to regulation, not a new substrate.

why.correct: The normal strain's pathway shuts down when isoleucine is plentiful. The changed enzyme 1 ignores isoleucine, so the pathway keeps running and wastes raw materials and energy.
options: Without feedback inhibition, the pathway runs whether or not the product is needed.
The data show the changed enzyme is far less sensitive (93% at 5.0 mM against 4%).
The normal strain switches its pathway off; the changed strain cannot, so the two differ.
The changed enzyme works at full rate with nothing added (100%), so its active site is intact.

why.correct: If the last step were blocked, the first four would keep running and intermediates would pile up. Blocking the first step saves the starting material and the energy spent on every step.
options: Shutting the entrance saves material and energy along the whole pathway.
Every enzyme in the pathway has an active site.
Inhibiting the last enzyme would lower isoleucine production, not raise it, but would still waste the earlier steps.
Inhibition slows a pathway; it does not change ΔG or speed anything up.

why.correct: Percent decrease = (100 − 22) ÷ 100 × 100 = 78%.
109 + 47 = 156 kJ, exactly the energy in the glucose. No energy appeared or disappeared; it changed form.
options: The budget balances, which is what conservation of energy predicts.
Losing energy as heat fits the second law, but comparing the two numbers does not test it; the sum is what these data show.
Heat cannot be used to make ATP; the energy for building cells came from breaking down glucose, and the heat is what was lost.
The data show energy amounts, not whether glucose use stopped or what stopped it.

why.correct: By the second law, every conversion releases some energy as heat. That spread-out energy raises disorder and cannot be gathered back to do a cell's work.
options: Heat is the disordered, unusable end form of energy in cells.
Energy is never destroyed; the calorimeter measured it.
Heat is energy (molecular motion), which is why it is counted in kJ.
Heat is not used to make ATP; ATP is made with energy from breaking down glucose.

why.correct: Staying ordered (repairing molecules, keeping gradients) takes a steady energy input. After stored fuel runs out, order is lost and the cells die.
options: Order needs constant energy input; without it the second law wins.
Molecules wear out and gradients leak; keeping them takes energy, which needs food.
Energy cannot be created, and heat cannot be used to drive cell reactions.
Cells first break down their own stored fuel, releasing heat, before they die.

why.correct: No conversion is 100% efficient: some energy always ends up as heat, and entropy (disorder) increases.
options: This is the second law: conversions release heat and raise disorder.
This is the first law, conservation of energy.
Whether a reaction releases energy says nothing about its speed; that depends on activation energy.
Cells build local order only by releasing heat that raises disorder elsewhere even more.

why.correct: Building a large molecule from small ones is anabolic, and it needs energy (endergonic); cells drive it with ATP and other phosphate-carrying molecules.
options: Building molecules uses energy, supplied by coupling to ATP hydrolysis.
Breaking proteins down is catabolic; building them is not.
Building a protein needs energy; it does not happen on its own.
Building is anabolic, and it is driven by ATP being used up, not made.

why.correct: Glucose's hydrogen atoms, with their electrons, end up on oxygen in water. Glucose loses electrons (oxidized), oxygen gains them (reduced), and electrons moving toward oxygen release energy.
options: Glucose gives up electrons; oxygen, which pulls electrons strongly, accepts them.
This reverses the direction: glucose loses electrons, it does not gain them.
Oxygen gains electrons, so it is reduced; and the products hold less energy than the reactants.
Atoms are conserved, but electrons shift between them, which is what a redox reaction is.

why.correct: 50 kg ÷ 50 g = 1,000. A small pool is recycled about a thousand times a day: ATP is a short-term carrier. Long-term stores are fat and glycogen.
options: The ratio shows rapid recycling of a small pool.
50 g is a tiny store; it would last about a minute at that rate of use.
ADP and Pi are recycled into ATP; the parts are reused, not made new.
The energy to remake ATP comes from food; 50 kg of ATP per day needs far more than 50 g of food.

why.correct: In coupling, an exergonic reaction (ATP hydrolysis) drives an endergonic process (moving ions uphill, doing mechanical work).
options: Pumping against a gradient needs energy, supplied by ATP hydrolysis.
Muscle movement is work driven by ATP hydrolysis.
Evaporation is a physical change with no reaction driving another.
Diffusion down a gradient needs no energy input, so nothing is coupled.
Heating is energy transfer, not one reaction driving another.

why.correct: With no way to remake ATP, the ATP-ADP cycle stops: ATP falls, ADP rises, and the processes coupled to ATP hydrolysis, such as pumping ions, fail.

variables.name: ATP concentration in the cell
variables.why: ATP keeps being hydrolyzed for work but is no longer remade, so its level falls.

variables.name: ADP concentration in the cell
variables.why: Each ATP hydrolyzed leaves an ADP, and ADP is no longer turned back into ATP, so it builds up.

variables.name: Concentration difference of sodium ions across the membrane
variables.why: The pump that keeps sodium out needs ATP; as ATP runs out, sodium leaks in and the difference shrinks.

variables.name: Number of sodium-potassium pump proteins in the membrane
variables.why: The pumps are still there over a few minutes; they stop working because they lack ATP, not because they are destroyed.

why.correct: Making ATP is endergonic (+30.5 kJ/mol), so it is coupled to energy-releasing breakdown of fuel molecules.
options: Breaking down food releases the energy that recharges ADP to ATP.
Building proteins uses energy; it cannot supply it.
Heat cannot drive cell reactions; it is energy that is no longer usable.
Using one ATP to make another gains nothing: the energies cancel, and some is lost as heat.

why.correct: The action spectrum dips to 25-35% between 525 and 575 nm, the green part of the spectrum, where the pigments absorb least.
options: The action spectrum is lowest here, at 25-35% of maximum.
Blue light gives 85-90% of the maximum rate.
Red light gives 85-90% of the maximum rate.
Violet light gives 55-85% of the maximum rate.

why.correct: Chlorophyll b (60%) and carotenoids (80%) absorb strongly at 475 nm. As accessory pigments in the light-harvesting complex, they pass absorbed energy to the reaction center's chlorophyll a.
options: Accessory pigments widen the range of light a plant can use.
Shorter wavelengths do carry more energy per photon, but a photon must be absorbed to be used, and chlorophyll a absorbs few here.
Water is split at photosystem II's reaction center, not by carotenoids on their own.
At 550 nm the cells' rate (25%) is still low, so measuring living cells does not raise the rate everywhere; the pigments explain the pattern.

why.correct: At 550 nm the action spectrum is 25%, against 90% at 450 nm. Less absorbed light means less ATP and NADPH and less sugar.
options: Light that is not absorbed cannot drive photosynthesis.
Reflected light is the light the cells do not use; green algae look green because they reflect it.
The same intensity is not the same absorbed energy; absorption differs hugely between the two wavelengths.
Carotenoids pass absorbed energy on to chlorophyll a; they help rather than block.

why.correct: The bacteria follow O₂, and O₂ release is highest in blue (425-475 nm) and red (650-675 nm) light, matching the action spectrum.
options: These are the parts where the action spectrum, and so O₂ release, peaks.
Green and yellow light give the lowest O₂ release.
O₂ release varies strongly with wavelength, so the bacteria will not spread evenly.
Energy per photon matters only if the photon is absorbed; the action spectrum at 400 nm (55%) is below the blue and red peaks.

why.correct: Rate = (0.80 − 0.18) ÷ 20 min = 0.62 ÷ 20 = 0.031 absorbance units per minute (a decrease).
DCPIP loses its color when reduced. In the light, chloroplasts pass electrons from water through the light reactions to DCPIP instead of NADP⁺.
options: The dye was reduced by electrons flowing out of the light reactions.
Isolated chloroplasts in this setup have no CO₂ source mentioned, and sugar does not reduce DCPIP; the color change tracks electron flow.
Tube D, DCPIP in the light without chloroplasts, stayed at 0.80, so light alone does not bleach it.
Nothing suggests uptake of dye; boiled chloroplasts (tube C) left the dye in solution, pointing to a working process, not absorption.

why.correct: Tube A and tube C differ only in boiling. Boiling denatures proteins such as the photosystems, and tube C's absorbance barely changed.
options: Only boiling differs, so the comparison tests whether intact, folded proteins are needed.
Tube A and tube B differ in light, so they show that light is required.
Tube A and tube D differ in whether chloroplasts are present at all, not in whether their proteins work.
Neither tube B nor tube D changed, and they differ in two ways (light and chloroplasts), so this comparison tests nothing clearly.

why.correct: With electrons stuck at photosystem II, it cannot accept more from water, so water splitting and O₂ release stop. No electrons reach the cytochrome complex, so H⁺ pumping stops too, and the gradient for ATP fades.
options: A block anywhere on the chain stops flow along all of it, including water splitting at the start.
Photosystem II splits water only to replace electrons it has passed on; if it cannot pass them on, splitting stops.
ATP synthase needs the H⁺ gradient that electron transport builds.
Photosystem I receives electrons from the chain that starts at photosystem II, not from water; tube E's dye barely changed.

why.correct: Electrons from photosystem I normally reduce NADP⁺ to NADPH. DCPIP stands in for NADP⁺ and changes color when reduced.
options: NADP⁺ is the natural final acceptor of the light reactions' electrons.
O₂ is released by water splitting; it does not accept these electrons in photosynthesis.
CO₂ is reduced later, in the Calvin cycle, by NADPH, not directly by the light reactions.
ATP is made by ATP synthase using the H⁺ gradient; it does not accept electrons.

why.correct: At 0-20% light the means differ by 0.5 or less and the error bars overlap. From 40% up, the 0.10% curve is higher by 4-9 µmol/m²/s with no overlap.
options: Same at low light, different at high light: that is the pattern.
At 10% light the values are 3.0 and 3.2, nowhere near double.
This reverses the curves: 0.04% levels off near 9.6, while 0.10% keeps rising to 18.3.
In the dark net uptake is −1.5: the leaf releases CO₂ rather than taking it up.

why.correct: At 10% light, adding CO₂ changes nothing (3.0 against 3.2) but more light raises uptake, so light limits. At 80% in normal air, more light changes nothing (9.5 to 9.6) but extra CO₂ nearly doubles uptake, so CO₂ limits.
options: A limiting factor is the one whose increase raises the rate; that is light at 10% and CO₂ at 80%.
At 10%, extra CO₂ barely helps; at 80%, extra light barely helps.
At 80% the curve for normal air is flat, so more light does not help there.
At 10% the two CO₂ levels give the same uptake, so CO₂ is not limiting there.

why.correct: Plant cells carry out cellular respiration all the time. In the dark nothing offsets it, so the leaf gives off CO₂ and net uptake is negative.
options: Respiration continues in light and dark; only photosynthesis needs light.
The Calvin cycle builds sugar from CO₂; breaking sugar down is cellular respiration, a different pathway.
The value stays at −1.5 at steady state in both CO₂ levels, matching ongoing respiration rather than a stored pool emptying.
Both curves give the same −1.5 with small error bars, which is a real, repeatable value, not an error.

why.correct: Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (18.3 − 9.6) ÷ 9.6 × 100 = 90.6%, which rounds to 91%.
With light and CO₂ both high, the limit shifts to the enzyme reactions of the Calvin cycle, and enzymes slow down at low temperature (fewer energetic collisions).
options: Temperature becomes the limiting factor when light and CO₂ are plentiful.
Respiration does slow, but it is small (1.5); the much larger slowing of the Calvin cycle dominates.
Temperature also affects photosynthesis, through its enzymes.
Light absorption by pigments hardly depends on temperature; enzymes slow, but the leaf does not stop.

why.correct: Only sample 1 had a gradient (inside pH 4, outside pH 8), and only it made much ATP, in the dark. This supports chemiosmosis: the H⁺ gradient itself drives ATP synthesis.
options: The gradient, not light, was the energy source; light normally just builds the gradient.
Sample 1 made 100 nmol of ATP in the dark.
Sample 2 was also moved to pH 8 but had no gradient, and made almost none.
In sample 1 the inside (pH 4) was more acidic, with more H⁺, than the outside.

why.correct: ATP synthase makes ATP only as H⁺ pass through it. If H⁺ can cross anywhere, they run down the gradient by the leak, and its energy is lost as heat.
options: A leak lets the gradient run down without passing through ATP synthase.
The chemical acts on membranes; nothing suggests it destroys ADP or Pi.
The stem says the chemical makes membranes leaky; sample 5's drug acts on ATP synthase itself, a different mechanism with the same result.
Raising pH makes a solution less acidic; and leaking H⁺ out would raise the inner pH toward 8, erasing the gradient.

why.correct: pH 4 to pH 9 is a 10⁵-fold difference in H⁺ concentration, against 10⁴ for pH 4 to pH 8. A steeper gradient drives more H⁺ through ATP synthase.
options: More stored energy in the gradient means more ATP.
pH 9 is close to the normal stroma pH of about 8, not an extreme that would denature the enzyme.
The amount of ATP depends on how much H⁺ flows, which depends on the size of the gradient.
Nothing in the setup makes pH 8 special; any outside pH higher than the inside gives a gradient.

why.correct: In light, electron transport pumps H⁺ and makes ATP anyway. Keeping them dark removes that source, so any ATP must come from the pH difference the researchers created.
options: Removing light removes the normal way the gradient is built, isolating the variable being tested.
Pigments absorb light, not ATP.
Splitting water would also be driven by light, but the main reason is to stop all light-driven electron flow, including H⁺ pumping; the buffer holds pH steady.
The Calvin cycle does not need darkness; it needs ATP and NADPH, and it is not present in isolated thylakoids anyway.

why.correct: The Calvin cycle's enzymes are in the stroma, and it spends ATP (energy) and NADPH (electrons) to reduce CO₂ to sugar.
options: Stroma, ATP and NADPH: all three are right.
The thylakoid space collects H⁺; O₂ is a waste product the Calvin cycle does not use.
Light and water are used by the light reactions, not by the Calvin cycle.
The Calvin cycle makes sugar from CO₂; it does not use O₂ or glucose.

why.correct: Water splitting (2 H₂O → 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻ + O₂) is the source of the O₂ released. The oxygen atoms of CO₂ end up in sugar and water made by the Calvin cycle.
options: Labeled water gives labeled O₂: the classic evidence that O₂ comes from water.
The Calvin cycle keeps the oxygen of CO₂ in its products; it releases no O₂.
All the O₂ released comes from water.
Cells use heavy isotopes normally; that is why the labels can be traced.

why.correct: Circular DNA like a bacterial chromosome, bacteria-like ribosomes, a double membrane and photosystems matching those of cyanobacteria all point to a cyanobacterial ancestor taken in by endosymbiosis.
options: Shared, specific molecular features are the evidence for common ancestry.
Plant cells have mitochondria too, and where chloroplasts occur says nothing about where they came from.
Most bacteria are not green, and color alone is weak evidence.
Most bacteria cannot photosynthesize, so this claim is false.

why.correct: The light reactions make ATP, NADPH and O₂; the Calvin cycle uses the ATP for energy and the NADPH for electrons.
options: ATP supplies energy for carbon fixation and for regenerating the cycle's starting molecule.
NADPH supplies the electrons that reduce CO₂ to sugar.
O₂ is released as a by-product; the Calvin cycle does not use it.
CO₂ comes from the air, not from the light reactions.
Glucose is made from the Calvin cycle's products; it is not an input.

why.correct: Light-independent means light is not absorbed by the cycle's own steps. But the cycle depends on the light reactions' ATP and NADPH, which run out soon after dark.
options: No light means no new ATP and NADPH, so the Calvin cycle slows and stops.
The Calvin cycle uses the light reactions' products; stopping them starves it.
Nothing suggests light damages these enzymes; they work during the day.
The cycle does not absorb light itself; the problem in the dark is lack of ATP and NADPH.

why.correct: Darkness stops the light reactions at once (no O₂, no new gradient), and the Calvin cycle follows as its ATP and NADPH run out. The pigments themselves stay.

variables.name: O₂ released by the chloroplasts
variables.why: Without light, photosystem II stops losing electrons, so water is no longer split and no O₂ is released.

variables.name: H⁺ concentration in the thylakoid space
variables.why: Electron transport stops pumping H⁺ in, while H⁺ keeps flowing out through ATP synthase, so the gradient runs down.

variables.name: Rate of CO₂ fixation by the Calvin cycle
variables.why: As ATP and NADPH from the light reactions run out, the Calvin cycle slows and stops.

variables.name: Amount of chlorophyll in the leaf
variables.why: Pigments are not used up in a few minutes; the leaf keeps the same chlorophyll whether or not light is shining.

why.correct: Electron transport releases energy in small steps; the cytochrome complex uses it to pump H⁺ into the thylakoid space. ATP synthase then uses the H⁺ gradient to make ATP (chemiosmosis).
options: Energy goes into the H⁺ gradient first, then into ATP.
ATP is made by ATP synthase from the gradient, not directly at the cytochrome complex.
CO₂ is never split; the O₂ comes from water at photosystem II.
Heat cannot be used to do the cell's work, and the energy is captured in the gradient instead.

why.correct: Corrected volume = 0.84 − 0.02 = 0.82 mL. Rate = 0.82 mL ÷ 20 min = 0.041 mL/min.
Respiring peas take in O₂ and give out CO₂. If the CO₂ stayed as gas the two would nearly cancel; KOH absorbs the CO₂, so the shrinking volume measures O₂ used.
options: Removing CO₂ lets the volume change track O₂ uptake.
KOH absorbs CO₂; it does not produce O₂.
The water bath holds the temperature; KOH has a chemical job.
KOH is there to absorb CO₂; nothing in the setup is aimed at bacteria.

why.correct: Beads do not respire, so any movement in their tube comes from physical changes. Subtracting it corrects every vial at that temperature.
options: Beads-only vials are a control for physical changes in gas volume.
Glass beads are not alive and use no O₂; any reading is a physical change.
Each vial is separate; beads in one vial do nothing for peas in another.
The beads-only vials contain no peas at all.

why.correct: A germinating seed is growing: it needs ATP, so it oxidizes its stored food quickly, using O₂. A dry seed's cells are nearly inactive.
options: Active growth needs ATP, which comes from respiration using O₂.
The vials are sealed and the peas are seeds; dry peas have no green leaves to photosynthesize, and the dry-pea vial shows a little uptake, not a release.
The vials hold the same total volume, and peas do not absorb KOH; the drop moves because O₂ is used.
Dry seeds do have mitochondria; their respiration is very slow, not absent (0.06 mL in 20 minutes).

why.correct: Lower temperature means slower molecules and fewer energetic collisions, so enzyme-catalyzed respiration slows (to about 39%). Below the enzymes' optimum, warming speeds it up.
options: Enzyme rates rise with temperature up to their optimum, so 30 °C would likely be faster.
Cold slows enzymes but does not denature them; warming restores the rate.
Seeds in a dark sealed vial do not photosynthesize; they simply respire more slowly.
KOH works well at both temperatures; the beads-only correction already accounts for physical effects.

why.correct: From 10 to 14 min, O₂ fell from 140 to 20 nmol/mL: 30 per minute, the steepest slope.
options: After DNP, the slope is steepest: 120 nmol/mL in 4 minutes.
With ADP, O₂ fell 80 nmol/mL in 4 minutes (20 per minute), fast but not fastest.
After oligomycin, O₂ fell only 12 nmol/mL in 4 minutes.
After cyanide, O₂ stayed at 20: no use at all.

why.correct: Rate = (232 − 152) ÷ (6 − 2) = 80 ÷ 4 = 20 nmol/mL per minute.
Pumping and H⁺ return are linked. With the return route blocked, H⁺ piles up in the intermembrane space until pumping becomes too hard, and electron flow to O₂ slows almost to a stop.
options: A too-steep gradient holds back the chain: respiration is tied to ATP synthesis.
The stem says oligomycin blocks ATP synthase; and adding DNP later restores fast O₂ use, so the chain still works.
ATP synthase makes ATP; it does not release O₂.
Electrons go to O₂, not to ADP; and the drop happens right when oligomycin is added.

why.correct: DNP is an uncoupler: it lets H⁺ back into the matrix without ATP synthase. The gradient stays low, so the chain pumps and uses O₂ at full speed, while ATP synthase stays blocked by oligomycin.
options: Uncoupling separates electron flow from ATP synthesis; the energy is released as heat.
Oligomycin is still present, so ATP synthase stays blocked; DNP gives H⁺ another way back.
DNP's effect is to move H⁺, and O₂ use stops at once when cyanide is added, showing the chain, not DNP breakdown, uses the O₂.
The stem says DNP carries H⁺, not electrons.

why.correct: Cyanide blocks the last protein of the chain, the one that hands electrons to O₂. With no electrons reaching O₂, O₂ use stops, whatever happens to the gradient.
options: Blocking the final transfer to O₂ stops O₂ use directly.
The stem says cyanide blocks the last protein of the chain, not DNP.
O₂ stays flat at 20 nmol/mL after cyanide, so nothing is using it up.
ATP synthase was already blocked by oligomycin; cyanide acts on the chain.

why.correct: 3.80 mmol CO₂ ÷ 1.90 mmol glucose = 2.0, matching alcohol fermentation: glucose → 2 ethanol + 2 CO₂.
With O₂: 0.45 × 30 ≈ 13.5 mmol ATP. Without: 1.90 × 2 = 3.8 mmol ATP. 13.5 ÷ 3.8 ≈ 3.5, while glucose use was 0.45 against 1.90.
options: Respiration with O₂ gets far more ATP from each glucose.
1.90 × 2 = 3.8 mmol is less than 0.45 × 30 ≈ 13.5 mmol.
CO₂ is not a measure of ATP; the two pathways release different CO₂ per ATP.
Glycolysis still makes 2 ATP per glucose during fermentation.

why.correct: Glycolysis needs NAD⁺ to accept electrons. Without O₂, NADH cannot unload at the chain, so it gives its electrons to a molecule made from pyruvate, which becomes ethanol. The NAD⁺ released keeps glycolysis going.
options: Fermentation's job is to recycle NAD⁺, not to make extra ATP.
Fermentation makes no ATP beyond glycolysis's 2.
Fermentation does not use the electron transport chain at all.
The flask with O₂ made almost no ethanol (0.02 mmol), so ethanol is not made regardless.

why.correct: 2.70 ÷ 0.45 = 6.0: all six carbons of each glucose left as CO₂, the result of glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle.
options: Six CO₂ per glucose is complete oxidation of all six carbons.
The ratio is 6, not 2, and almost no ethanol was made.
This divides glucose by CO₂ instead of CO₂ by glucose.
The carbon in CO₂ comes from glucose; O₂ accepts electrons and becomes water.

why.correct: Without UCP1, brown-fat mitochondria made 28% of the normal heat, and the mice cooled to 31.0 °C against 36.4 °C; the error bars do not come close.
options: Lower heat output and lower body temperature both point to UCP1's role in heat production.
UCP1 lets H⁺ bypass ATP synthase, so it reduces ATP made per O₂; its job is heat.
Brown-fat mitochondria were isolated from both groups, so these mice do have brown fat; other tissues were not measured.
Their body temperature was 5.4 °C lower, so they did not keep it as well.

why.correct: Without ADP, ATP synthase cannot run and the gradient would normally build and slow the chain. UCP1 gives H⁺ another way back, so the chain keeps running and its energy is released as heat.
options: An H⁺ leak frees the chain from waiting on ATP synthesis.
UCP1 is a channel for H⁺; it makes no ATP.
UCP1 moves H⁺, not electrons; the chain still passes electrons to O₂.
Mice lacking UCP1 used far less O₂ under the same conditions, which points to UCP1, not stored ADP.

why.correct: Each H⁺ that leaks through UCP1 is an H⁺ that does not turn ATP synthase. More O₂ is used per ATP, and the difference is released as heat.
options: Uncoupling lowers ATP made per O₂ used.
Fast O₂ use here is driven by the leak, not by ATP synthesis.
The ratio depends on how much H⁺ goes through ATP synthase, which UCP1 reduces.
Heat comes from the leak; it does not make ATP synthase produce more ATP.

why.correct: Without ADP, ATP synthase cannot make ATP, so H⁺ cannot return through it. Normally the gradient would then stall the chain. Fast O₂ use in that condition shows a leak; comparing the two groups ties the leak to UCP1.
options: Removing ADP takes ATP synthase out of the picture, isolating the leak.
ADP does not react with the fuel; it is a substrate of ATP synthase.
ATP synthase needs ADP; without it, no ATP is made.
Nothing suggests ADP is toxic; it is a normal substrate in every mitochondrion.

why.correct: The Krebs cycle's enzymes are dissolved in the matrix, inside the inner membrane, as are those of pyruvate oxidation.
options: The matrix holds the Krebs cycle enzymes.
Glycolysis happens in the cytosol.
The electron transport chain and ATP synthase are in the inner membrane.
The intermembrane space is where H⁺ accumulates.

why.correct: The carbons of glucose leave as CO₂ in pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle, and the CO₂ is breathed out.
options: Glucose's carbons become CO₂, which is exhaled.
Water forms from O₂, electrons and H⁺; it contains no carbon.
O₂ contains no carbon, and the rat takes it in rather than giving it out.
Urea carries nitrogen from amino acids; glucose has no nitrogen.

why.correct: Each pyruvate loses one carbon as CO₂ in pyruvate oxidation, and the Krebs cycle releases the remaining two per acetyl CoA: 6 CO₂ per glucose in all.
options: One CO₂ per pyruvate, 2 per glucose.
Two CO₂ per acetyl CoA, 4 per glucose.
Glycolysis splits a six-carbon sugar into two three-carbon pyruvates; no carbon is lost.
The chain moves electrons and H⁺; it releases no carbon.
Lactic acid fermentation turns pyruvate into lactate, keeping all three carbons; alcohol fermentation in yeast does release CO₂.

why.correct: Muscle fermentation turns pyruvate into lactate using NADH's electrons, freeing NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue. It happens in the cytosol and makes no extra ATP.
options: Regenerating NAD⁺ is the whole point of fermentation.
Fermentation gives only glycolysis's 2 ATP per glucose.
Fermentation does not use the electron transport chain.

why.correct: Blocking the final transfer to O₂ stops the chain, the gradient and most ATP synthesis; cells fall back on glycolysis and fermentation.

variables.name: O₂ used by the cells
variables.why: Electrons can no longer be passed to O₂, so O₂ is not reduced to water.

variables.name: H⁺ concentration in the intermembrane space
variables.why: With electrons stuck, the chain stops pumping H⁺, while H⁺ keeps flowing back through ATP synthase, so the gradient runs down.

variables.name: ATP made by oxidative phosphorylation
variables.why: ATP synthase needs the H⁺ gradient, which is fading.

variables.name: Lactate made by the cells
variables.why: NADH can no longer unload at the chain, so cells turn to fermentation to regenerate NAD⁺ for glycolysis, making lactate.

variables.name: Number of mitochondria in each cell
variables.why: Cyanide blocks a protein; it does not destroy mitochondria or make new ones within minutes.

why.correct: Fatty acids are long chains of –CH₂– groups: highly reduced, with lots of electron-rich hydrogen. Cut into acetyl CoA, they load many NADH and FADH₂, which drive more oxidative phosphorylation.
options: More electrons per gram means more NADH and FADH₂, so more ATP.
Fats are made of glycerol and fatty acids, not glucose.
Fatty acids are broken down in the mitochondria, and ATP synthase sits in the inner membrane.
Most ATP from fat comes from the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.

why.correct: Both pump H⁺ into a compartment separate from where ATP is made (thylakoid space, intermembrane space), and ATP synthase makes ATP as H⁺ flows back into the stroma or matrix.
options: The two systems mirror each other; the H⁺ store and the ATP-making side are on opposite sides of the membrane.
H⁺ is pumped away from the ATP-making side and flows back to it through ATP synthase.
This reverses the electron sources: water in chloroplasts, food molecules in mitochondria.
This reverses the acceptors: NADP⁺ in chloroplasts, O₂ in mitochondria.

why.correct: Glycolysis needs a steady supply of NAD⁺. Without O₂ to accept electrons, NADH piles up and NAD⁺ is used up; with no fermentation to recycle it, glycolysis stops.
options: The NAD⁺ supply links glycolysis to O₂ indirectly.
Glycolysis does use 2 ATP to start, but it makes 4, so it does not depend on the chain for ATP.
Nothing suggests a fast pH crash; the immediate problem is the missing NAD⁺.
Pyruvate cannot turn into O₂; this is not a real reaction.
